title: Intergenerational Associations in Intergroup Contact and the Moderating Role of Self‐Expansion Motivation Among Ethnic Minority Adolescents in China
abstract: Objectives Intergroup contact is widely recognized as an important means of reducing bias and promoting positive intergroup relations among children and adolescents. However, less is known about whether and how parents′ intergroup experiences are reflected in their children′s own intergroup contact, particularly in non‐Western settings. This study examined intergenerational associations in intergroup contact among Tibetan adolescents in China and further tested whether self‐expansion motivation moderated these associations. Method Adolescents reported perceived parental contact quality, their own contact intention, contact quantity, contact quality, and self‐expansion motivation. Latent profile analysis was used to identify self‐expansion motivation profiles. Separate regression models were estimated for each profile, and regression coefficients for perceived parental contact quality were compared across profiles using coefficient‐difference z tests. Results Three self‐expansion motivation profiles were identified: low (21.1%), medium (41.9%), and high (37.0%). Higher perceived parental contact quality was associated with stronger contact intention, greater contact quantity, and better contact quality among adolescents. Self‐expansion motivation moderated the associations of perceived parental contact quality with contact intention and contact quality: These associations were significant in the medium and high‐motivation profiles, but not in the low‐motivation profile. In contrast, self‐expansion motivation did not moderate the association between perceived parental contact quality and contact quantity. Conclusions The findings suggest that adolescents′ perceptions of parental intergroup contact are associated with their own intergroup contact in a non‐Western ethnic minority context. They also indicate that adolescents′ self‐expansion motivation may help explain when perceived parental contact quality is more strongly associated with adolescents′ own intergroup contact.

journal.name: New Directions for Child and Adolescent Development
